name: Purple Madder
lede: Purple madder was a deep, purple-leaning madder lake sold by the English colourman George Field in the early nineteenth century.

sections.title: Field's purple
sections.body: The Pigment Compendium says Purple madder is another name for Field's purple, a madder lake made by the English colourman Field, who called it purple leading to marrone [1]. Osborn, in 1845, gives madder purple, purple rubiate and Field's purple as terms for madder lakes of this kind [2]. Salter, in 1869, describes purple madder as a transparent, dark crimson-leaning lake [3].

sections.title: Why painters wanted it
sections.body: Field wrote in 1835 that it was a very rich, deep carmine made from madder, not a brilliant purple, and preferred it to the purple of gold and to burnt carmine for its richness, durability and transparency [4]. Salter agreed in 1869, calling it the only durable organic purple on the palette [4]. Salter's caveat was that it was available only in small quantities [4]. For the dye plant behind it, see [[madder]].

sections.title: On a modern shelf
sections.body: A modern table of artists' paint names in Baty's book lists a Purple Madder in a table that also includes Winsor Violet and Permanent Mauve [5]. The swatch here is a muted red [3][5]. Its place beside [[purple]], [[mauve]] and [[tuscan-red]] shows how far the screen swatch sits from the old lake's name [3][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our name graph records purple madder from Maerz and Paul in 1930 [6]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings it appears in 119 paintings, 0.5 per cent, and in 106 by the within-painting measure [7]. It is more common than 59 per cent of the named colors and peaks in the 1400s, in 16 of 945 paintings, 1.7 per cent, or 2.8 times the expected rate [7]. In 86 per cent of those 106 paintings it plays an accent [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test, and the 1400s peak predates Field by centuries [7].
